incite

/in-SYT/ - rhymes with night · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Incite means to stir others up toward violent or unlawful action.

Recruiters moved from table to table in the tavern, inciting men who an hour before had wanted nothing but their supper.

Worked Example

Chroniclers of the tax revolt give preacher Amos Kale a careful sentence of his own. For a year his sermons called the land tax wicked — hot words, and only words. Then, on the last Sunday of Lent, he ended by naming the hour the assessor's cart would reach the ford, and by Monday the cart was in the river. The revolt had found its first act, and Kale, who never left his pulpit, had supplied its time and place.

Incite is the exact word for that last sermon, because to incite is to stir others up toward violent or unlawful action — the inciter supplies the heat and the direction, and other hands do the rest. A year of preaching had merely made the tax hateful. One sentence told hatred where to stand and when.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

stir up: To stir up is the plain kitchen phrase for setting people or feelings in motion — trouble implied, law optional; you can stir up gossip, dust, or a whole town. Incite is the statute's word: the crowd must be pushed toward something violent or unlawful, nothing less.

whip up: To whip up is to work a crowd's feeling to a froth — excitement, fury, panic — and the phrase stops at the feeling. Incite goes the further step: the stirred crowd is pointed at a violent or unlawful act, and the pointing itself is what the law punishes.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

defuse: takes the spark out of the crowd before it lands

quiet: settles the room back into itself

Where it sits · how unlawful the pushed act becomes — urge → egg on → incite

urge vs. incite: Urge is open, lawful pressure, nowhere near incite — a coach urges the runner on, and nobody calls a constable.

egg on vs. incite: Egging someone on goes further than urging — the pusher wants the stunt for the spectacle of it; incite claims the most: the push aims at something unlawful, and the law counts the pusher among the guilty.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-

Prefix — in-: in, on

Root — cit

Root — cit: to set in motion, to rouse (Latin citare)

Put it together

Put it together: In- (on) + cit (to set moving) = to set moving against. Latin citare meant to rouse or summon into motion, and incitare spurred horses. English kept the spurs: what you incite was standing still until you dug in and pointed it somewhere.

Use the root in a new word: excite

Use the root in a new word: excite: Excite is the same rousing root turned inward — ex- (out) + cit: feelings called out into motion.

Word Choice

formal / legal, accusatory

Incite lives in criminal statutes and referees' reports, and it needs three things: a pusher, a crowd, and an unlawful or violent aim. Instigate, its unit-mate, works one quarrel and often works it in whispers; incite is loud and aimed. The act built to draw rage is a provocation, and language built for the purpose is incendiary.
